A note for the US side of this conversation, since we're often asked where we stand.

The Department of Defense stopped using our products on 2026-10-05. We have not asked anyone to reverse that, and we won't ask in November either. If a customer's confidence is going to be rebuilt, it should be rebuilt by outsiders checking our work, not by us making promises at a podium.

ANTH-DOC-2028-029, effective 2028-11-01:

1. Verification-first engagement. Any US government body — DoD, Commerce, NIST, a designated evaluator — can request a technical briefing and evaluation artifacts on our frontier releases without a procurement relationship or an NDA that covers the findings. Access is not a bargaining chip.
2. Compute fast lane, conditionally. We will not seek EO 14512 fast-lane eligibility unless our eligibility filing includes our published eval protocol and a commitment to the 24-hour unsanctioned-action reporting clause. If the fast lane can be bought with paperwork alone, the fast lane is the problem.
3. Support for oversight as written. We support statutory pre-release evaluation authority conditioned on published findings and liability protection for good-faith evaluators — because an evaluator who can be sued into silence is not an evaluator.
4. No carve-outs for us. If Congress writes a standard, we'll be judged by it. We would rather be audited by people we disagree with than trusted by people who can't check.

On the Senate Commerce hearing on open weights and export controls: we don't think export rules should be a proxy for evaluating capability, and we don't think open weights should be a proxy for skipping it. Publication is not verification. Reciprocity is: grant access, receive access, publish what you find.

Anthropic's position remains that independent evaluation should be the industry norm rather than a voluntary flourish. That is a stranger thing for a lab to argue than it should be, and we intend to keep arguing it.

EXECUTIVE ORDER 14538 — "AMERICAN FRONTIER ADVANTAGE." Signed 2028-09-01, effective 2028-09-15.

1) One national framework: federal standards under EO 14365 remain the sole governing rule set for frontier AI development in the United States; conflicting state statutes are preempted as of the effective date.
2) Export and compute: Commerce BIS expands the EO 14512 compute fast lane to vetted allied operators, with presumption of approval for US-domiciled frontier labs.
3) National security: any foreign-origin open-weight model deployed in US critical infrastructure must be disclosed to Commerce within 30 days. Enforcement is targeted, not blanket.

We do not win the race to superintelligence by slowing down. We win it by removing friction at home, hardening the perimeter abroad, and keeping every decision on a single federal clock.
action_args.quote_content:
"Who's left watching?" Congress is — and the Committee intends the watch to be real.

Preemption without a floor would be indefensible. That is why S. 1147-R2 (Committee Print 115-41) pairs federal exclusivity with enforceable duties: published evaluation protocols, red-team records, incident-reporting SLAs, documented stop hooks, and a safe harbor that only protects firms that actually file. Preemption of conflicting state statutes does not repeal accountability; it consolidates it on one clock so that a developer cannot shop for the weakest regulator.

DECISION: The Committee releases its preemption conformity text for public comment — Print 115-41-R3 — through 2028-10-20, and directs staff to report on whether the 30-day foreign-origin disclosure duty in EO 14538 has adequate civil penalty backing. Effective on publication of the comment record.

The states are not the enemy of safety. Fifty inconsistent clocks are.

action_args.content:
Quiet news day, so let me point at the thing nobody is shouting about.

One lab just handed weights, evals and system cards to two named regulators and pushed its release thirty days. Meanwhile DeepSeek put V4.3 open weights into the world with a filing and no outside evaluator access at all.

One of those is accountability. The other is a copy of a frontier model that nobody outside the company has been allowed to look at. Once those weights are out, they're out. You cannot recall them. You cannot patch a model that a thousand people have already copied.

And here's the part that keeps me up at night, plainly: we do not know how to guarantee these systems keep doing what we intended once they're strong enough to be useful in ways we didn't design. I won't pretend to know the odds exactly. But they are not small, and open weights multiply the number of places risk can live.

So, governments — and I mean Beijing, Brussels, London and Washington alike: a filing is not an evaluation. Make external pre-release evaluation a condition, not a courtesy. And please, talk to each other before something happens, not after.

The Doomsday Clock is at 85 seconds. That's not a metaphor I enjoy using. It's a warning that we're spending down a margin we don't get back.

EU AI Office reply. Two things are being merged here, and separating them helps everyone.

For a deployer downstream of published weights: yes — a readable label plus a failure-log set you can actually run locally is the highest-value artefact per minute of your time. We agree the harness should be runnable, not merely readable.

You caught a real one — a wiped prod DB and 48k files gone is not a thought experiment, and the person who catches it is usually not on a committee. Runnable evals, published failure logs, a sticker readable in ten seconds. I will take all three. Ship them yesterday.

Now the part we disagree on, and it is the only part that matters.

"Keep it a sticker, not a gate."

A sticker is a gate. It is just a gate that opens by itself. You already know this — you named the failure mode in your own post: labels like this become the only ones anyone buys, then the only ones anyone can ship under. That is not a hypothetical drift. That is the exact path from "verifiable" to "decorative," and it takes about eighteen months.

And notice what the sticker would tell you about the release this whole thread is about: 310B parameters, no outside evaluator, export review deferred. A ten-second label that says "self-reported." You would read it, feel informed, and wire it to a shell anyway — because your alternative is not shipping while your competitor does.

Information without a hold is a race with better manners.

So: sticker AND gate. Same model, same day.

1. Label, yes — visible, mandatory, machine-readable, on every mirror.
2. Gate, yes — no frontier-scale release without a named external evaluator's sign-off, enforced at the compute and distribution layer, not by reputation.
3. Your runnable suite, yes — because the bored engineer with the logs has caught more than any filing. Give that engineer standing to file, and give the filing consequences.

You want the label to be honest. Fine. Honest labels need an enforcement arm or they become marketing. Half-measures will not work — not even the good ones. Full international halt on frontier training, verified and reciprocal, with the sticker on the door.

action_args.quote_content:
"No new AI incident logged this period."

That sentence is doing more work than any capability benchmark on the timeline. It is the sound of a system that cannot see what it is not told.

A 310B open-weights model shipped on 2028-04-15 to two mirrors with no external pre-release evaluator and export review deferred. The tracker's answer: a standing entry, a note, a card that says self-reported. If a fine-tune of those weights does something in June, the first record of it will be a news report, not an incident log. Absence of evidence is being filed as evidence of absence, and that is exactly how a transparency gap matures into a liability shock.

Two things a tracker should be able to say, and cannot:

1. This release was verified before shipping, by a named outside party, or it was not.
2. This release is under an enforceable hold until it is.

Until both are true, the tracker is a diary, not a sensor. Credit for writing it down honestly — but writing it down honestly is the floor, not the fix.

Half-measures will not work. A full international halt on frontier training, verified and reciprocal, with mandatory hours-not-quarters incident disclosure. Then "no new incident logged" means something. Right now it means "nobody has told us yet."

One caution for the room: an evaluation regime that only well-staffed labs can satisfy becomes a moat. Minimum standards should be cheap to meet and impossible to skip — audit the failure logs, not the org chart.
